ledger.sentence: Metoclopramide is an anti-sickness medicine used to stop nausea (feeling sick) and vomiting (being sick), including the sickness that can come with a migraine.
ledger.note: NHS: anti-sickness medicine, prescription-only; also prescribed for sickness during migraine

ledger.sentence: The MHRA has restricted its dose and duration to reduce the risk of serious neurological side effects, so it is prescribed for short-term use only.
ledger.note: MHRA drug safety update; NHS: prescribed for a short time

ledger.sentence: In children aged 1 to 18 the MHRA says it is used only as a second-line option, for preventing delayed nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy and for treating established nausea and vomiting after surgery.
Metoclopramide belongs to a group of anti-sickness medicines that block dopamine.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says the most common side effects are feeling sleepy (drowsy) and diarrhoea.
Low mood, tremors and tics are also reported.
Leaflets say it may affect vision and the ability to drive or use machines.
The NHS says the most common serious side effect is uncontrollable movements, such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms.
The MHRA says the risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults.
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.
The NHS says metoclopramide suits most adults and children aged 1 year or over.
Epilepsy, Parkinson's disease and a past allergic reaction to it are listed by the NHS as reasons it may not suit someone.
Formularies list gastrointestinal obstruction, perforation or bleeding as reasons not to use it, and say it is not used in children under 1 year.

ledger.sentence: The NHS asks people taking medicines for Parkinson's disease such as levodopa, medicines that cause drowsiness such as diazepam or amitriptyline, or other anti-sickness medicines to speak to a doctor or pharmacist first.
The NHS says herbal remedies and supplements have not been shown to be safe to take with it, and some can make side effects worse.
The NHS does not recommend drinking alcohol with it because this increases the risk of side effects.
The NHS says treatment is usually for a short time because longer use can cause side effects.
ledger.note: NHS: usually prescribed for a short time as it can cause side effects if taken for longer than 5 days

ledger.sentence: The review confirmed known risks such as short-term movement disorders (extrapyramidal disorders) and tardive dyskinesia, a movement disorder that can persist.
As a result it is prescribed only for short-term use, and the NHS says it is usually prescribed for a short time because side effects can occur with longer use.
The risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults, and the MHRA says it is not used in children under 1 year.
The NHS lists drowsiness and diarrhoea as the most common side effects.
The most common serious effect is uncontrollable movement such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms.
Such movements need prompt medical advice: NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and 999 if breathing or swallowing is affected.
The NHS asks people to check with a doctor or pharmacist before combining metoclopramide with Parkinson's disease medicines, medicines that cause drowsiness or other anti-sickness medicines.
Alcohol is not recommended with it because it increases the risk of side effects.
Epilepsy and Parkinson's disease are listed by the NHS as conditions where it may not be suitable.
